extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and students of poetics/creative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing and judging tragic drama and epic narrative: plot construction, character, recognition, diction, style, and metre, with examples and anti-patterns. Useful for playwrights and poets seeking classical principles of poetic composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter: tragic families and great error or frailty
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect tragedy should be founded on the story of a few houses and on persons who have committed or suffered some great error or frailty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best tragedies come from a limited set of moving family histories (e.g., Alcmaeon, Oedipus, Orestes). This is why a few families furnish the subjects of tragedy; poets should seek such material and apply their art to it rather than telling any random legend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic pleasure: pity and fear through imitation, not spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure proper to Tragedy is that which comes from pity and fear through imitation; these emotions may be aroused by spectacle, but the inner structure (incidents) is the superior and proper means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on spectacular or monstrous effects to produce emotion, because spectacle is extraneous and less artistic. The plot should produce the impression even when merely heard (example: Oedipus). Spectacle may create shock but not the true tragic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot intelligibility by narration alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot ought to be so constructed that, even without the aid of the eye, a listener will be moved with horror and pity at what takes place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design incidents so their emotional force emerges from their internal logic and sequence; test the plot by imagining it told aloud without staging (Oedipus as exemplar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of incidents: kinship/friendship ties heighten pity
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions capable of arousing pity or terror should occur between persons who are friends, near, or dear to one another (e.g., brother and brother, son and father, mother and son).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an enemy kills an enemy, little pity is excited beyond the suffering itself. Therefore select situations of close personal relation to maximize tragic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skillful handling of received legends
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should not destroy the framework of received legends but ought to show invention of his own and skilfully handle the traditional material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain essential facts of tradition (e.g., who killed whom) while introducing poetically appropriate novelties and arranging incidents so as to impress tragic quality upon the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of the tragic deed and their effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragic deed may occur (1) consciously with knowledge of persons; (2) perpetrated in ignorance with discovery afterwards; (3) the agent is about to act with knowledge and then refrains; (4) about to act in ignorance and discovers before acting. The best is perpetration in ignorance with later discovery; the worst is intending to act knowingly and then not acting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer incidents where the deed is done in ignorance and recognition follows (produces startling effect without gratuitous shock). Avoid cases that shock without producing disaster or dramatic resolution (e.g., 'about to act, then not'). Examples: Medea (knowingly does deed), Oedipus (done in ignorance), Cresphontes/Merope (recognition at point of slaying).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot causality: necessity/probability and prohibition of internal Deus ex Machina
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should make events follow by necessary or probable sequence; the unravelling and complication must arise out of the plot itself. The 'Deus ex Machina' must not be used to bring about events within the action proper, only to report or account for antecedent/subsequent events outside human knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid irrational solutions inside the drama (internal deus ex machina). If irrational must appear, keep it outside the scope of the tragedy. Examples of misuse: Medea, certain returns in the Iliad; proper use: as a reporter of divine knowledge beyond the drama's action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character aims: goodness, propriety, truth to life, consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Character should aim at four things: (1) it must be good (moral purpose), (2) it must be proper (appropriate to gender/status/type), (3) it must be true to life (distinct from goodness/propriety), and (4) it must be consistent (even inconsistent characters must be consistently inconsistent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A speech or action manifesting moral purpose expresses character. Propriety cautions against incongruous traits (e.g., manly valour in a woman), and consistency protects against unexplained character degradation or sudden, unjustified shifts. Examples of faults: Menelaus' motiveless degradation, inconsistent Iphigenia portrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraiture: ennoble types while preserving likeness
rubrics_metrics.description: In representing characters, the poet should preserve the distinctive form of the original type yet ennoble it—make the likeness true to life but more beautiful or elevated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model after good portrait-painters: retain the type (irascible, indolent, etc.) but render it elevated. Example: portrayals of Achilles by Agathon and Homer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis): types and ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions vary in artistry: (1) recognition by signs/tokens (least artistic), (2) recognitions invented by the poet (artificial), (3) recognition by memory (object sight or song evokes recognition), (4) recognition by reasoning, and (composite) false inference. The best recognitions arise naturally from the incidents themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer recognitions that emerge from the plot's incidents (e.g., Oedipus, Iphigenia). Tokens and formal proofs are less artistic and may feel contrived. Examples: Odysseus' scar (token), Iphigenia's letter, recognition by minstrel's song.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization and stagecraft: place the scene before the eyes
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing plot and diction, the poet should place the scene vividly before his eyes to discover what is in keeping and to avoid inconsistencies; the poet should also work with appropriate gestures so actors' emotions are convincing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagining the scene as a spectator helps spot stage-level details and prevent oversights (example: Carcinus' failed piece due to an unnoticed fact). Use gestures and delivery as natural expressions of feeling; delivery belongs to a related art but informs diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot planning: outline then fill with relevant episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether using a ready-made story or constructing one, the poet should first sketch the general outline (single action with beginning/middle/end) then fill in episodes and amplify, ensuring episodes are relevant to the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the general plan to guide episodes (Iphigenia, Odyssey examples). Episodes give extension (Epic uses episodes more expansively) but in drama they must remain relevant; avoid adding irrelevant material that obscures unity (Odyssey vs tragedy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy structure: complication and unravelling; reversal and recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy has two parts—Complication (from beginning to the turning-point) and Unravelling/Denouement (from the change to the end). Complex tragedies depend on Reversal (peripeteia) and Recognition (anagnorisis); other types include Pathetic, Ethical, and Simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify clearly the turning-point and ensure both knot-tying (complication) and untying (unravelling) are done well; aim to combine many poetic elements (reversal, recognition, suffering) for greater effect. Test identity of a tragedy by comparing its complication and unravelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope constraint: avoid epic multiplicity in drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not turn an epic structure (multiplicity of plots, vast narrative) into a tragedy; a drama should focus on a single action. Attempting to dramatize a whole epic (e.g., the Iliad) or an entire large tale leads to failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a single portion or episode rather than the whole story. Examples of failure: dramatizations of the whole Fall of Troy or complete Niobe story; Agathon's failure for taking too much material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as an integral actor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as one of the actors and an integral part of the whole, sharing in the action rather than acting as mere interludes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model the Chorus after Sophocles where it contributes to the subject of the piece; avoid treating choral songs as unrelated interludes (a fault of later poets like Agathon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (ideas) in drama: speech must produce effects; incidents should speak
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought includes proof and refutation and the stirring of feelings (pity, fear, anger) or suggestion of importance; dramatic incidents should produce effects on their own, while speeches must generate intended effects by what is said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat incidents and speeches from the perspective of the emotions and reasoning they are meant to produce; do not reveal essential Thought apart from what the speaker conveys—speech should perform its persuasive or emotional work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and modes of utterance: part of delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Modes of utterance (command, prayer, statement, threat, question, answer, etc.) fall within diction but mainly belong to the art of Delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While detailed execution is delivery's province, the poet should be aware of these modes and use them appropriately; misuse is not a fatal poetic error but belongs to performance technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style balance: clarity without meanness; mix current and unusual words with moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean: use a mixture of current/proper words for clarity and rare/metaphorical/ornamental words for elevation. Excess of either plainness or strangeness is faulty (riddle or jargon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infuse rare words, metaphors, lengthenings, contractions, and alterations in moderation to gain distinction without obscurity. Critics who denounce such licenses err when they ignore propriety and moderation. Examples: contrast Aeschylus and Euripides lines where the rarer term elevates diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of metaphor and word choice as marks of genius
rubrics_metrics.description: A command of metaphor is the greatest stylistic quality and cannot be imparted by teaching; good metaphors require an eye for resemblances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate the aptitude for apt metaphorical analogies; metaphors raise diction when appropriate and are critical for certain genres (e.g., iambic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-word fit: choose words suitable to metre and genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Different word types suit different genres: compound words best for dithyrambs, rare words for heroic poetry, metaphors for iambic; heroic poetry tolerates rare words and metaphors more readily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match diction to the metre and genre: heroic/metre allows stately diction and rarities, while iambic seeks language nearer to familiar speech (often prose-level words).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic unity and scale: single action, appropriate length, and use of episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry should, like tragedy, be built on a single action whole and complete with beginning, middle, and end; its scale may be larger but must still keep the beginning and end within a single view. Episodes can diversify and add mass if relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt an epic so vast it lacks unity; detach a single portion and admit other events as episodes. Homer is the model: he selects portions rather than attempting the entire war story at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper metre selection: heroic for epic; avoid mixing metres
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic metre is most fitting for epic narrative (stately, massive), while iambic and trochaic tetrameter suit dramatic lyric/action. Mixing metres on a great scale is incongruous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metre by nature and genre; heroic verse admits rare words/metaphors, iambic/trochaic are more stirring or akin to dance. Historical example: Chaeremon's ill-advised mixing of metres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator reserve: the poet should speak little in his own person
rubrics_metrics.description: In epic the poet should speak as little as possible in his own person, because imitation, not authorial intrusion, is the poet's proper role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit authorial commentary or self-address; let characters and incidents provide the imitation and narrative authority.
